 Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Harris and Democratic challenger Dan Schwartz are vying to represent Maryland’s 1st Congressional District. Both candidates were asked to respond to a series of questions about their priorities and the issues facing the district. Their answers follow.
 Andy Harris 
 Incumbent Andy Harris has been in office since 2011.
 Photo courtesy of Maria Sofia. 
 Incumbent Congressman Andy Harris (MD-1), 69, is married and has five children. He received his undergraduate, medical, and master’s degrees from Johns Hopkins University and has been an anesthesiologist, served in the Navy Medical Corps and the U.S. Naval Reserve as a commander on active duty during Operation Desert Storm.
 Q: Congressman Harris, you’ve represented this district since 2010 and chair the House Freedom Caucus. What’s your assessment of your time in congress and why should constituents bring you back?
 A: I’ve represented the First District since 2011, which has included the Eastern Shore during that time. My job has been to protect the things that make the Shore work: the Bay, the poultry industry, farms, the watermen, and the tourism industry. As chairman of the House Appropriations USDA subcommittee, I determine where federal dollars for our farmers and rural communities get spent. In that role, I have been able to get well over $100 million for our Eastern Shore infrastructure, including the new hospital, water and water treatment projects, first responder needs such as the Easton fire training center, and volunteer fire company needs. If re-elected, I would work to continue to bring funding back to the district.
 Q: The district’s economy runs heavily on farming and the Chesapeake Bay seafood industry. What’s one concrete federal policy, on trade, labor, or environmental regulation, you’d push to support those industries, and what trade-offs would you accept to get it?
 A: These industries run on labor that can’t be sourced locally with American workers. That’s why I’ve been the leader in Congress on expanding the H2B temporary foreign worker program that seafood processors depend on, as well as an advocate for expanding the H2A temporary foreign agricultural worker program. The sad truth is the Americans will not do these jobs (and temporary jobs should not be the goal for American workers) — so we need temporary foreign workers badly if these core industries for the Shore are to survive.
 Q: Rural hospitals and healthcare access are a recurring issue on the Shore. What specific step would you take in Congress to address it, and how would you pay for it?
 A: As a physician who practiced on the Middle Shore, I know that it is increasingly difficult to recruit health care workers to rural areas. That’s why I’m the only member of the Maryland Congressional delegation to vote for the $50 billion Rural Health Care Transformation Fund as part of the Working Families Tax Cut Act. This fund will help pay for rural health care facilities on the Shore, as well as fund strategies to improve rural health and healthcare delivery. The cost of that Fund was entirely paid for by eliminating waste, fraud, and abuse in federal programs such as Medicaid and food stamps.
 Q: Maryland’s congressional map has been the subject of legal and political fights. Where do you stand on how this district’s lines should be drawn, and would you support changes even if they made your own race harder?
 A: Extreme partisan gerrymandering is wrong, and Wes Moore is wrong to try to return Maryland back to the pre-Hogan days of Maryland’s congressional map being the worst gerrymandered in the nation. Everyone who agrees should vote against Question 3 on the ballot this fall.
 Q: How do you plan to stay accessible to constituents across a sprawling district that includes the Shore, Cecil and Harford counties, and part of Baltimore County, and what’s one thing about how the seat has been represented that you’d do differently?
 A: Because the district is so large and new technology has become available, we have turned to that technology to make sure everyone has access if they don’t see me when I travel through the district. This year alone, I’ve held numerous telephone town halls reaching tens of thousands of constituents from the Lower Shore to Cecil, Harford and northern Baltimore counties. These virtual electronic town halls allow people to stay at home, cook and eat dinner, and still be able to ask a question or hear others ask questions just as in a physical town hall. In addition, although this is a sprawling rural district, no one has to drive much more than an hour to reach one of my three district offices.
 Q: Maryland’s first district has seen a major rise in Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests over the past few years. How do you plan on working with ICE if elected?
 A: Unfortunately, the Eastern Shore was the target destination for thousands of people illegally crossing our southern border during the wide-open border policy of the Biden administration. I support enforcing immigration law and cooperating with federal partners. I applaud Wicomico County for joining ICE through the Warrant Service Officer program under 287(g), which helps ensure that criminal illegal aliens are turned over safely to federal custody instead of being released into the community. I oppose the sanctuary policies of the Moore administration.
 Dan Schwartz 
 Dan Schwartz is running for congress in Maryland’s 1st district.
 Photo courtesy of Ralph Alswang. 
 Hopeful Dan Schwartz, 37, is married to Megan Harmer who is a family nurse practitioner, and has three children, Henry, Eddie and Noa. He received his Bachelor’s in Political Science from George Washington University and went to the Graduate School of Banking in Colorado. Schwartz was the senior director of Nonbank Supervision & Enforcement until he quit his job to run for Congress in April of last year.
 Q: Congressman Harris has represented this district since 2010 and chairs the House Freedom Caucus. What’s your assessment of his voting record over that time, and what specifically would you do differently if you held the seat?
 A: His voting record has put extremist politics ahead of working families across MD-1. His votes for the tariffs and war in Iran has financially crippled families and endangered the lives of our service members. As your congressman, I’ll work to roll back the devastating cuts to our rural hospitals and Medicare which Rep. Harris voted for in the Big Beautiful Bill. I’ll also work to preserve and strengthen Social Security which so many of my constituents rely on. Rep. Harris is part of a small group of members that attempted to cut nearly half a billion dollars from its operating budget.
 Q: The district’s economy runs heavily on farming and the Chesapeake Bay seafood industry. What’s one concrete federal policy, on trade, labor, or environmental regulation, you’d push to support those industries, and what trade-offs would you accept to get it?
 A: I would roll back haphazardly placed tariffs on our trading partners. They’ve raised costs for fertilizer, and closed international markets, putting farmers already under stress in an even worse position. There were many soybean farmers, including here in Talbot County, who were unable to get a crop in the ground last year. We will enact deliberate trade policies that support our farmers, pass a farm bill that increases subsidies without making disastrous cuts to SNAP, restore funding to lending programs farmers rely on, and rehire staff at NOAA and USDA who assist our farmers and watermen in doing their jobs.
 Q: Rural hospitals and healthcare access are a recurring issue on the Shore. What specific step would you take in Congress to address it, and how would you pay for it?
 A: I will fight to reverse the cuts from the BBB to Medicaid, Medicare, and long-term care programs. These cuts kick in after the mid-terms because Republicans knew they would devastate rural America. We have great healthcare providers throughout MD-1 like my wife who is a Family Nurse Practitioner. We need to make it easier for people to become nurses and to live and buy homes in our communities. We must defend against efforts to negate the professional classification of nurses which are simply a gift to the private student lending industry. Our communities need more providers. Not more predatory debt.
 Q: Maryland’s congressional map has been the subject of legal and political fights. Where do you stand on how this district’s lines should be drawn, and would you support changes even if they made your own race harder?
 A: I am disappointed in Annapolis politicians choosing to push for further gerrymandering in the state. If they were truly interested in preserving our democracy they would have pushed for open primaries instead. Our closed primary system only pushes us to further political extremes. The way to beat Rep. Harris is at the ballot box this year instead of kicking the can down the road. I will be voting against the ballot initiative that would further empower the state legislature to gerrymander the state.
 Q: How do you plan to stay accessible to constituents across a sprawling district that includes the Shore, Cecil and Harford counties, and part of Baltimore County, and what’s one thing about how the seat has been represented that you’d do differently?
 A: I am committed to holding monthly in-person town halls with the option to attend virtually. Rep. Harris has not held one in 3 years and will occasionally throw together last minute telephone town halls where he talks down to his constituents.
 Q: Maryland’s first district has seen a major rise in Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests over the past few years. How do you plan on working with ICE if elected?
 A: I believe our government has the ability to conduct immigration enforcement in a rational and ethical manner that respects our constitution. If a violent offender is here illegally, local law enforcement should coordinate with federal immigration officials to keep our neighbors safe. Despite rhetoric, nothing in the Community Trust Act prevents this coordination. We should not require local police to do the work of federal immigration enforcement officials at traffic stops or court appointments. We do not need immigration officials rounding up people working as caregivers, for example, who are midway through legal immigration processes.
